statement: In the same 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly and were not seeking treatment (one double-blind, placebo-controlled inpatient laboratory study), the morning after the highest of three single intranasal doses, compared with the morning after placebo, is associated with lower self-ratings of feeling alert, content, friendly, social and talkative, a faster heart rate (90 against 78 beats per minute) and higher blood pressure (diastolic 79 against 69 mm Hg), with methamphetamine still measurable in the blood after every dose. Ratings of feeling depressed, feeling anxious and wanting methamphetamine did not change, and no effect was detected on tests of attention, memory and reaction speed; the paper gives no numbers for those tests and tested only once in the morning, so only a large impairment could have been detected. After the two lower doses, only one of the tabulated mood ratings changed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: The morning after the highest dose in a small hospital study, people felt less alert, content and friendly than after a dummy dose, and their heart rate and blood pressure were still higher. They did not feel sadder or more worried and did not want methamphetamine more. Memory and attention tests showed no change, but the study was small, tested only once that morning and did not print the test results. Lower doses changed little the next morning.
population: Adults aged 22 to 45 (2 women, 9 men) with DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse or dependence who used it mainly intranasally, were not seeking treatment and had no other psychiatric disorder; studied as inpatients
exposure: A single intranasal dose of methamphetamine the previous day (three dose levels; amounts and times are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's morning after placebo
outcome: Next-morning mood and drug-effect ratings, craving, cognitive and psychomotor performance, heart rate, blood pressure and plasma methamphetamine
magnitude: Highest dose against placebo (100-point scales): alert 38.1 against 55.6; content 37.4 against 53.9; friendly 43.0 against 65.0; social 40.8 against 67.1; talkative 37.4 against 58.5 (each marked p < .05); heart rate 90.5 against 78.4 bpm; systolic 124 against 118 and diastolic 78.6 against 69.0 mm Hg (p < .05). After the lowest dose, 'social' 50.4 against 67.1 (p < .05); no other tabulated mood rating, heart rate or blood pressure changed significantly after the two lower doses. Depressed, anxious and craving ratings unchanged and no significant performance effect (no values reported).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.2 Subjective effects; Table 1, subjective-effect rows
evidence.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose, against placebo: alert 38.09 against 55.55, content 37.36 against 53.91, friendly 43.00 against 65.00, social 40.82 against 67.09, talkative 37.36 against 58.46 (marked p < .05); energetic 22.80 against 35.20 marked only as different from the lowest dose; 'social' also lower after the lowest dose (50.36; F = 4.46).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.4 Physiological measures; Table 1, physiological rows
evidence.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose: heart rate 90.46 against 78.36 bpm, systolic pressure 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg (all p < .05 against placebo); plasma methamphetamine still measurable after all three active doses.

No significant residual effect on the digit-symbol, repeated-acquisition, divided-attention, rapid-information and digit-recall tasks (no means or statistics given); ratings of 'depressed', 'anxious' and 'I want meth' were not altered by the previous day's dose (no values given).

The authors note that mood and performance were measured at only one morning time point, that subtle performance effects might need repeated testing through the day, that only single doses were studied, and that the persisting cardiovascular elevation may matter for toxicity with repeated use.

risk_of_bias.note: Selective reporting (no numbers for performance or for the unchanged mood items) and possible unblinding for self-ratings.

indirectness.note: Worded for single laboratory doses in experienced people.

imprecision.note: Eleven people; the absence of a performance effect is not precise.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high. Risk of bias -1 (self-rated mood by participants who may have recognised the dose; performance and several mood results reported without numbers). Imprecision -2 (11 people, one morning test, no intervals; the null performance result cannot exclude moderate effects). Very low. Single study.
